description: A timeline comparison of the cable-video bundle era collapsing under streaming disruption—measured with real subscriber counts and revenue pressure.
youtube_description:
📺 **Cable’s Last Stand** — How pay TV kept losing the bundle while streaming stacked wins.

In this chart-race style video, we track how the US pay TV subscriber base shrank over 2010–2025 while major streaming services scaled—turning the “cord-cutting” story into a measurable timeline.

**Chapters**
00:00 2010–2013: Pay TV still dominates
00:55 2014–2016: Early streaming gravity
01:50 2017–2019: The bundle cracks
02:50 2020: The acceleration year
03:40 2021–2022: Streaming scale hits escape velocity
04:35 2023–2025: Mature churn, new equilibrium

**What to watch for**
- The steep pay TV decline after 2016
- Netflix + Prime Video rising like a counterweight
- Hulu steady lift as the “second screen” habit grows
- Disney+ arriving later and reshaping the competition

**Call to action**
If you want more chart-race data stories like this, **subscribe** and drop a comment with the year you think cable’s “last stand” truly began.

instagram_caption:
📉 Cable’s Last Stand is playing out in slow motion—until it isn’t.

In 2010, the US pay TV world was still massive: about **101.0M** subscribers (cable + satellite). For years, the bundle felt untouchable—until streaming turned “convenience” into a habit. This chart race starts with stability… and quickly becomes a countdown.

By **2014**, pay TV was **95.5M** subscribers, and the early streaming era was no longer “experimental.” Netflix isn’t even the same scale of threat in the early 2010s—but once it passes into mainstream binge territory, it becomes a real alternative. In this dataset, Netflix jumps from **33M (2014)** to **71M (2019)**, while pay TV slides from **95.5M to 76.8M** in the same window.

Then the real drama: **2016–2019** is where the cracks widen. Pay TV drops from **88.0M (2016)** to **76.8M (2019)**, while Hulu rises from **15M (2016)** to **34M (2019)**—showing that consumers weren’t just “dropping cable,” they were **rebuilding their channel lineup** with streaming.

The turning point hits hard in **2020**, when pay TV falls from **64.8M (2020)** in the dataset’s jump window, while Prime Video keeps climbing (from **77.5M in 2020 to 83.0M by 2025**). By **2021**, Disney+ is already at **118M**, and by **2022** it peaks at **161M**—reshaping the competitive landscape even as pay TV keeps hemorrhaging down to **~45.8M by 2025**.

The bundle didn’t die overnight. It just lost the “default” status—then couldn’t regain it.

💬 **Which do you think mattered most in cable’s collapse: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, or Prime Video—and why?**

facebook_caption:
Cable’s Last Stand compares the decline of US pay TV subscribers (cable + satellite) against the rise of major streaming ecosystems. In 2010, pay TV sat at roughly **101.0M** subscribers. Over the next decade, the subscriber base eroded as streaming adoption scaled: pay TV falls to **95.5M (2014)**, **88.0M (2016)**, and **76.8M (2019)**. 

The disruption accelerates around 2020 as consumers increasingly shift to streaming-first viewing. Pay TV in the dataset drops to **~64.8M (2020)**, while Netflix rises to **~74M (2020)** and continues toward **~96M (2025)**. Hulu climbs steadily from **~15M (2016)** to **~60M (2025)**, reflecting the emergence of “second-screen” streaming behavior. Prime Video also increases from **~77.5M (2020)** to **~83.0M (2025)**. 

Disney+ reshapes the late-stage competition after launch: it reaches **~118M (2021)** and peaks near **~161M (2022)** in the dataset, before settling around the mid-150s by 2024–2025. By the end of the timeline, pay TV is down to **~45.8M**, illustrating how the bundle lost dominance and never fully recovered.

Which single company do you think had the biggest role in breaking the pay TV bundle? Comment with your pick and your reason.
